The Mottled grouper (Mycteroperca rubra) is a relatively large serranid inhabiting the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean, where adults commonly reach an extreme total length of 144 centimeters [Li = 144 centimeters]. This substantial ultimate size is accompanied by a relatively high asymptotic wet weight of 33,600 grams [Wwi = 33,600 grams], a value derived from length–weight relationships typical for groupers of this genus. In the Gulf of Gabès and adjacent waters, field studies have documented that the species exhibits a protracted somatic growth phase before initiating reproductive activity, with the total length at puberty determined to be 34 centimeters [Lp = 34 centimeters], which corresponds to an early maturation schedule relative to its maximum size. This pattern suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes the attainment of a size refuge from predation, a common feature among epinephelines, before substantial energetic investment in gamete production begins. Juvenile individuals, which are initially pelagic after the larval drift phase, gradually transition to structured benthic habitats, and their growth rates during these early years are rapid, enabling them to reach the pubertal threshold within a relatively short timeframe compared to other similarly sized serranids.

Reproductive output in Mycteroperca rubra has been characterized through histological examination of ovarian tissue from gravid females captured during the spawning season. At a sustained water temperature of 19.4 °C [T = 19.4 °C], a mature female can produce approximately 19.6 million oocytes per year [Ri = approximately 19.6 million oocytes per year], based on a fecundity of roughly 57,000 oocytes per gram of body mass and an asymptotic adult weight of 33,600 grams [Wwi = 33,600 grams]. This energetic investment reflects a continuous but seasonally pulsed spawning strategy across several months. The wet weight at birth is remarkably small, estimated at 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams] per individual, based solely on the diameter of the fertilized ovum and its associated yolk reserves prior to chorion rupture. Such a minute propagule mass is typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts that release numerous small eggs into the water column, where the ensuing yolk-sac larva must rely on endogenous nutrients until the onset of exogenous feeding.

Larval development in Mycteroperca rubra proceeds through a typical teleost sequence, beginning with the yolk-sac larva stage immediately following eclosion. The exotrophic transition, marked by first feeding and swim bladder inflation, occurs when the mouth gapes sufficiently to capture small planktonic prey, and the larvae subsequently enter the pelagic larval phase, dispersing widely in the current. Field observations from the Mediterranean coast indicate that the lifespan of this species can extend to 7,300 days [am = 7,300 days] under ambient thermal regimes that average 19.4 °C [T = 19.4 °C], a longevity that permits multiple iteroparous spawning seasons over many years. This extended lifespan is consistent with the general pattern among larger groupers, which tend to exhibit slow growth, late maturation, and considerable adult survival. During the juvenile stage following metamorphosis and benthic settlement, individuals remain in seagrass meadows and rocky outcrops, where they gradually accumulate the body mass necessary to reach the pubertal threshold and become reproductively viable members of the population.

The ultimate wet weight of 33,600 grams [Wwi = 33,600 grams] represents a considerable accumulation of somatic tissue over the species' long life, and this mass is typically attained only after several decades of sustained feeding on a piscivorous and crustacean diet. Comparative analyses with congeners such as Mycteroperca marginata reveal that Mycteroperca rubra occupies an intermediate position in terms of both maximum length and body mass, with its ultimate total length of 144 centimeters [Li = 144 centimeters] placing it among the mid-sized groupers of the temperate eastern Atlantic. The thermal dependence of physiological rates in this species is pronounced, and all of the key demographic parameters discussed here were derived from populations experiencing a mean annual temperature near 19.4 °C [T = 19.4 °C], which is typical of the shallow coastal waters where adults aggregate to spawn. Reproductive senescence has not been systematically documented, but the species' capacity for repeated spawning events over its long lifespan ensures a high cumulative fecundity across the adult phase.

Intraspecific variation in size at maturity has been noted across the geographic range of Mycteroperca rubra, with populations in the cooler waters off the Atlantic coast of Morocco tending to mature at a slightly larger total length than the 34 centimeters [Lp = 34 centimeters] reported from the warmer Mediterranean basin. This pattern is consistent with the temperature–size rule observed in many ectothermic vertebrates, where slower growth in cooler environments delays the attainment of the pubertal threshold. The estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams] per egg is a critical determinant of larval survival, as smaller propagules experience higher starvation risk during the yolk-sac stage and the early exotrophic period. Despite this vulnerable start, the high fecundity afforded by the species' large body size—exemplified by the ultimate wet weight of 33,600 grams [Wwi = 33,600 grams]—ensures that a sufficient number of offspring survive the planktonic bottleneck to maintain stable population dynamics under favorable oceanic conditions.
